title: Peace, be still (Mark 4:35–41)
hookLine: reading the storm again: why are you fearful

cards: Evening, at the end of the same long day of parables. Jesus has been teaching from a boat, and he says, let's cross to the other side. They push off, just as they are.

Then a great storm of wind rises, the waves beat into the boat, and it starts filling with water. Some of these men are fishermen; they know what a filling boat means. You've met this storm before, back in the stories.
Read in Mark's order, you can see where it falls.

teach.b: First, the sleeper. Mark gives a small, human detail.
In the Douay-Rheims: "And he was in the hinder part of the ship, sleeping upon a pillow; and they awake him, and say to him: Master, doth it not concern thee that we perish?"
A cushion in the stern, asleep after a day of teaching. And the disciples don't only ask for help. They ask, don't you care?
He gets up, rebukes the wind, and says to the sea: "Peace, be still." In Mark's Greek, be still is literally be muzzled, the same word he used when Jesus silenced a demon in Capernaum.
The wind stops, and there's a great calm. Third, the question to them.
"Why are you fearful? have you not faith yet?" Not yet. Mark's disciples are slow learners, and he doesn't hide it.
Fourth, their question. Now they're more afraid than they were in the storm, and they say to each other: "Who is this (thinkest thou) that both wind and sea obey him?"

teach.h: IN THE PSALMS, GOD RULES THE SEA.
teach.b: That question is why the path just spent five weeks in the Psalms. There, it's God who rules the sea and stills its waves; one psalm tells of God turning a storm into a breeze.

teach.h: WHO IS THIS THAT BOTH WIND AND SEA OBEY HIM?
teach.b: So when the wind obeys Jesus, the disciples are left staring at a question the psalms seem to answer. Mark doesn't answer it for them yet. He lets it hang there, in a quiet boat, in the dark.

how: Catholics hear the calming of the storm at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time; Pope Francis preached on this passage in an empty St. Peter's Square during the COVID-19 pandemic.

practice: Name this week's storm plainly, the bill, the diagnosis, the argument, the fear that wakes you, and picture it as wind and water in a small boat. If you pray, say the words into it slowly, peace, be still, as a prayer to Christ.
If you don't, say them to yourself, to your own racing mind, and let your breath slow.

wordCard.voice: Peace. The first word Jesus speaks to the storm: peace, be still. And the calm that leaves the disciples asking who he is. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: be silent, be muzzled, Jesus's words to the sea in Mark 4:39.

carryVoice: Your line: who is this. The week ran from sins first, through the sabbath, the twelve, a widened family, the sower and the sleeping seed, to a storm the wind obeys. Day two hundred three, done.
